query: For a CoCrFeNi high-entropy-alloy matrix evaluated in sliding from room temperature to 800 °C, what single intervention could overcome the difficulty of maintaining low coefficient of friction and wear rate throughout the full temperature range? Earlier studies of other self-lubricating material systems reported low coefficients of friction at 704 °C and favorable friction and wear behavior over broad temperature ranges. However, these results do not resolve the limited understanding of wide-temperature tribological performance in CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloys, and effectiveness must be maintained as operating temperature, load, and environment vary. Formulate one hypothesis that identifies a single intervention without presupposing its class, explains its mechanism, predicts friction and wear relative to the starting CoCrFeNi material, defines its temperature, load, and environmental boundaries, relates it to prior evidence, and specifies a controlled experiment with a clear result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Minor copper incorporation into the CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy matrix will promote the in situ formation of a stable, protective, copper-rich oxide tribofilm across a broad temperature range, which in turn will lower both the coefficient of friction and the wear rate from room temperature up to 800 °C relative to the undoped base alloy. This effect is mediated by the formation of a continuous, self-healing oxide layer that reduces direct asperity contact.
generation.material_initial_state: CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy produced with its typical microstructure (coarse or fine grain depending on processing) and exhibiting standard tribological behavior over the RT-to-800 °C range.
generation.intervention: Introduce a minor addition of copper into the CoCrFeNi composition.
generation.conditions: Dry sliding tests using a ball-on-disc or pin-on-disc configuration in ambient air, evaluated at various normal loads and sliding speeds at temperatures ranging from room temperature to 800 °C.
generation.structural_mediator: The intervention is expected to modify the chemical and microstructural evolution at the sliding interface by promoting segregation of Cu at grain boundaries or defect sites, which facilitates the formation of a continuous, adherent copper-rich oxide (or mixed oxide) tribofilm.
generation.mechanism: The presence of copper alters the oxidation kinetics such that a lubricious and self-healing oxide layer forms under frictional heating. This layer acts as a barrier to direct asperity contact, reducing shear stress at the interface, and simultaneously improves the local load-bearing capacity. At lower temperatures, the modified surface chemistry smooths the interface, while at elevated temperatures the stable oxide layer retains its protective, low-shear qualities.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline undoped CoCrFeNi alloy, the Cu-doped alloy will exhibit consistently lower friction coefficients and reduced specific wear rates across the entire temperature range. The beneficial effect should be observable as a reduction in friction fluctuations and less severe wear track damage (e.g., lower wear volume and fewer cracks) in tribological testing.
generation.baseline: The original CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy without any copper addition, which shows increased friction and wear rate fluctuations due to unstable oxide formation and microstructural softening at high sliding speeds and temperatures.
generation.boundary: The improvement is hypothesized to hold under dry sliding conditions in ambient air, across a temperature span ranging from room temperature (~25 °C) to 800 °C, under moderate-to-high normal loads and sliding speeds typical for engineering tribological applications.
generation.uncertainty: There is uncertainty regarding the optimum Cu content needed to balance phase stability with effective oxide formation, as well as the potential for unwanted segregation or embrittlement under certain sliding stresses and environmental conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one set of the standard CoCrFeNi alloy and a second set with a 5–10 at% Cu addition. Process both sets under identical conditions to achieve comparable microstructures. Conduct standardized dry sliding wear tests (e.g., pin-on-disc) under identical loads and sliding speeds at multiple temperatures (room temperature, intermediate temperatures, and 800 °C) in ambient air.
measurements: Measure the steady-state coefficient of friction continuously during sliding tests.
Quantify wear rates by measuring wear track volume using a 3D profilometer or white-light interferometry.
Analyze the worn surfaces using SEM/EDS and XPS to detect the presence, continuity, and composition of the oxide tribofilm.
Perform microstructural characterization (e.g., EBSD) to assess any changes due to Cu addition.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Cu-doped samples do not show a statistically significant reduction in both the coefficient of friction and wear rate compared to the baseline across the full temperature range, or if the oxide film is not observed to be more continuous or stable in post-test surface analyses, then the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractHigh-entropy alloys are known for their promising mechanical properties, wear and corrosion resistance, which are maintained across a wide range of temperatures. In this study, a CoCrFeNiCu-based high-entropy alloy, distinguished from conventional CoCrFeNi systems by the addition of Cu, which is known to enhance toughness and wear resistance, was investigated to better understand the effects of compositional modification on processability and performance. The influence of key process parameters, specifically laser power and scan speed, on the processability of CoCrFeNiCu-based high-entropy alloys produced by laser powder bed fusion additive manufacturing was investigated, with a focus of low laser power, which is critical for minimizing defects and improving the resulting microstructure and mechanical performance. The printed sample density gradually increases with higher volumetric energy density, achieving densities exceeding 99.0%. However, at higher energy densities, the samples exhibit susceptibility to hot cracking, an issue that cannot be mitigated by adjusting the process parameters. AbstractThe effect and mechanism of grain sizes on the tribological behavior of CoCrFeMnNi high entropy alloy (HEA) were studied by friction experiments and wear morphology analysis. Under normal low load and low sliding speed, the primary wear mechanism of the HEA samples is adhesive wear. With the increase in sliding speed, the wear mechanisms of the samples are adhesive wear and oxidation wear. The oxide layer formed under the action of friction heat of the coarse grain (CG) sample is easy to break due to the softening of the CG. With the increase of normal load and sliding speed, the wear mechanisms of the HEA samples are mainly adhesive wear, oxidation wear, and plastic deformation. The oxide layer of CG sample has many cracks, and the worn surface also has plastic deformation, which leads to the increase of friction coefficient and specific wear rate and the decrease of wear resistance. Therefore, the fine grain size HEA sample has better wear resistance than the CG sample due to its high surface strength.Keywords: high entropy alloy, grain size, tribological behavior, wear mechanism
